articles.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
articles.source: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
articles.summary: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space.

articles.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
articles.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

articles.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
articles.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

articles.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
articles.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
